articles.title: Bangladesh says it was not informed of its citizens' execution by Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia said it executed two Bangladeshis last week for committing an "indecent act" in a mosque.
articles.body:
Bangladeshi authorities say they were not informed of the recent execution of two Bangladeshi nationals in the holy city of Mecca until after it had taken place, local media reports.

A Bangladeshi man and woman were executed last Wednesday after being convicted of committing an "indecent act" inside a mosque, according to the Saudi interior ministry. The ministry did not specify the nature of the offending act.

Bangladesh says it has reached out to the Saudi Arabian government to ask for more details about the case.

The two Muslim countries share a close relationship due to their religious affinity and strong economic ties.

More than three million Bangladeshis work and live in Saudi Arabia, mostly in low-paying jobs, and news of the double execution has raised public concern in Bangladesh.

According to the Saudi interior ministry, the two Bangladeshi nationals were convicted and sentenced to death under "tazir", which in Islamic law refers to punishments left to the discretion of the judge.

The ministry statement said they were handed the sentences because of the severity of the offence, and the fact that they violated the "sanctity" of the mosque.

Bangladesh has reached out to the Saudi government about the offences involved and legal proceedings in the case, said state minister for foreign affairs Shama Obaed Islam.

The government would consider next steps, such as the repatriation of the bodies, after getting information from Saudi authorities, Islam said.

She added that the government was committed to safeguarding the welfare and interests of Bangladeshis abroad.

The two executed Bangladeshis were included in a list of prisoners that Saudi Arabia had shared with Bangladesh, upon a request from the Bangladesh Consulate General in Jeddah - but that list did not indicate that the pair had been sentenced to death, the Daily Star reported.

This is not the first time that foreign nationals have been executed by Saudi authorities.

According to Amnesty International, the country has executed around 100 people this year, many of whom are foreigners convicted of drug offences.

In 2011, eight Bangladeshi men were publicly executed in the Saudi Arabian capital of Riyadh after they were found guilty of killing an Egyptian.

Earlier this month, Saudi Arabia overturned a death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan man over a comment he had made on Facebook, which had led to him being convicted of blasphemy. That decision came after the case sparked public outcry in Sri Lanka and spurred diplomatic efforts to seek clemency for the man.

articles.title: Around 1500, artists in North India painted six scenes of Alexander the Great for an Iskandarnama manuscript; 526 years later, the illustrations sold in London for £70,760, more than 88 times the highest estimate
articles.summary: Around 1500, artists in North India painted six scenes of Alexander the Great; 526 years later, the illustrations sold for £70,760, over 88 times their
articles.body: Around 1500, artists in North India painted six scenes of Alexander the Great; 526 years later, the illustrations sold for £70,760, over 88 times their estimateSix small paintings created in North India around 1500, depicting episodes from the life of Alexander the Great, were reported to have sold for £70,760 at Lyon & Turnbull’s June 10, 2026, auction. The illustrations, made more than five centuries ago for a manuscript known as the ‘Iskandarnama,’ had been estimated at just £600 to £800. According to the official website of UK’s auction house Lyon & Turnbull, the six illustrations were produced during the Sultanate period in North India and came from a private collection in Spain. The reported price of £70,760 was more than 88 times the £800 high estimate.Six scenes from Alexander’s legendary journeysThe paintings illustrate different episodes involving Alexander, known as Iskandar in Persian literary tradition. The scenes include encounters with unusual beings, a meeting with an astrologer and a royal audience. According to Lyon & Turnbull’s catalogue, the illustrations depict Alexander meeting a hybrid human being; encountering male figures emerging from tall jars while riding a horse; consulting an astrologer; encountering a ‘makara,’ a mythical creature associated with the Eastern seas; riding alongside an attendant who waves a ‘chauri,’ or ceremonial fly-whisk, while receiving a bowing courtier; and scenes featuring a swirling ocean.The works are painted in gouache on paper. Each measures approximately 11 by 15.8 centimetres. The catalogue notes that the paper was cut down from a manuscript and mounted on brown paper. The auction house described the paintings as “vivacious illustrations”. It also noted their distinctive use of colour, particularly bright brick-red shades, and figures outlined in black with broad brushstrokes.What is the Iskandarnama?The ‘Iskandarnama,’ or Book of Alexander, belongs to a long literary tradition that retells the life and adventures of Alexander the Great. In Persian literature, Alexander is known as Iskandar, and stories about him combine historical elements with legendary encounters and philosophical journeys. The Iskandarnama is associated with the Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi and forms part of his ‘Khamsa,’ a collection of five narrative poems. Alexander’s story became a subject for illustrated manuscripts across regions influenced by Persian literary culture.These manuscripts combined written narratives with paintings that helped readers follow the stories. The six works sold in 2026 are surviving illustrations from such a manuscript tradition, rather than a complete book.Why the paintings are associated with the Sultanate periodLyon & Turnbull dates the illustrations to around 1500 and identifies them as works from the North Indian Sultanate period. According to the auction catalogue, the manuscript was commissioned by early sultans of Delhi, who retained Persian language, customs and Islamic religion. The auction catalogue links the manuscript to the Persian-language and cultural traditions retained by the early sultans of Delhi. Illustrated manuscripts offered a way to bring these stories into visual form, with artists adapting the narrative to their own techniques and colour choices.From a private collection in Spain to an auctionThe auction catalogue lists the illustrations as coming from a private collection in Spain. It does not provide a detailed account of when or how the six works entered that collection. Their appearance at Lyon & Turnbull’s June 2026 sale brought together a group of small paintings that had survived for more than five centuries.The sale does not establish who originally painted the illustrations or identify the individual artists. The auction house attributes them to North India during the Sultanate period, around 1500, rather than to a named painter. More than five centuries after they were made, the six scenes from Alexander’s legendary journeys were reported to have sold for a price far beyond the auction house’s estimate.You use AI every day. articles.title: Schools 'explosive device' email a hoax, says police
articles.summary: Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said police consider the risk to the public "as low".
articles.body:
An email threatening that "an explosive device" is located within hundreds of schools in Northern Ireland is being treated as a "hoax" by the Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI).

Assistant Chief Constable Ryan Henderson said police take "incidents of this nature very seriously" however "at this stage we consider risk to the public as low".

Some schools have closed after receiving the email, however others have decided to stay open and are taking advice from the PSNI.

Police Scotland said they are investigating emails sent to schools and are also treating threats as a hoax.

One school in Lambeg emailed parents to say that they should "come immediately" and collect children adding: "Please don't panic the children are all safe."

The email originated from outside the UK police say and similar emails have been received by some schools across the UK.

The PSNI said up to 300 schools have reported receiving the same emailed message which contained a generalised threat.

"Checks have not, at this time, resulted in anything untoward," added the PSNI.

"Based on enquiries and information to date, police are treating this email, which originated from outside the UK, as a hoax."

Henderson said police "understand the concern in the community, not to mention the disruption it has caused in some school communities and for students and parents".

"We will continue to liaise with schools impacted and have been working closely with the Department of Education and the Education Authority this morning to provide reassurance."

Police enquires into the email are continuing.

The Education Minister Paul Givan said the email has "caused huge alarm" and condemned the "level of disruption caused to young people's education".

In a statement he added: "Schools should continue to operate as normal."

"I recognise that this has caused huge alarm and distress among pupils, parents and school staff and I understand that schools have had to make decisions in the best interests of their pupils and staff. This has unfortunately led to a number of school closures.

"My Department will continue to work with the PSNI and the Education Authority and we will continue to engage with the PSNI as their enquiries continue."

Givan added: "I would like to thank school leaders, staff, pupils, parents and the PSNI for their cooperation and professionalism in responding to this incident."

At Rosetta PS in south Belfast, Chantal Ailsby told BBC News NI that the school handled the threat well.

Parents were given the option to collect their children from the school.

Nora Xhemha also collected her children.

"We don't know what is going on. I hope that every child here is safe."

Claire Robinson, who is the head teacher at Holy Evangelists' Primary School in west Belfast, told BBC Radio Ulster's the Nolan Show that the advice schools have been given is "practically non-existent".

"There's been nothing from the Education Authority, there's been nothing from CCMS [Council for Catholic Maintained Schools], bar two letters that are more or less telling us absolutely nothing," she said.

Robinson said she feels that principals have been left to make the decisions themselves.

"We need guidance in the event these things happen.

"It's wholly unacceptable when we're dealing with children".

Meanwhile, the principal for Rathcoole Primary School in Newtownabbey, Emma Quinn, said that although her school is having a staff training day, it had gone into a lockdown procedure.

However, she said there has been "very little guidance, if no guidance, from the Education Authority".

"It's left to principals to make a very vital decision about the safety of their pupils and staff."

Quinn added that there has been conflicting advice provided to school principals.

Rob Kelsall, assistant general secretary of school leaders' union NAHT, said that "bomb threats made against schools are utterly unacceptable".

He paid tribute to school leaders and staff who acted with professionalism in "extremely difficult circumstances".

But he said it is "unacceptable that some have been left trying to reconcile differing and, at times, contradictory advice from multiple agencies while managing incidents of this seriousness".

Kelsall said NAHT has raised these concerns with Givan is liaising with the police.

"We are calling for a joined-up review of how information is communicated to schools during incidents such as these so that leaders can have confidence that advice is timely, consistent and aligned."

The Education Authority (EA) has been contacted in regards to the critical comments made by Quinn, Robinson and the NAHT.

On the actual email itself, the EA said it was "aware" of it adding: "We recognise the concern this may cause for school leaders, staff, pupils and families.

"We are engaging closely with the PSNI and will act on their advice.

"Communications have been issued to schools, and we continue to support school leaders and keep them informed."

In a statement the Council for Catholic Maintained Schools (CCMS) said they recognise the message will have caused "concern and anxiety among pupils, parents and staff".

"We have advised any school that has received the threatening email directly to prioritise the immediate safety of pupils and staff and follow the advice and instructions of the PSNI and EA, alongside established emergency procedures."

They paid tribute to school leaders who "handled a distressing situation today with great calm and care".

"We will support every principal and Board of Governors in whatever decision they take for their own school community."

Similar threats were received by schools in the Republic of Ireland last week.

An Garda Síochána said it was "aware of a communication" that was sent on the 14 October.

"Gardaí are currently assessing the contents and credibility of that communication.

"Gardaí are engaging with a number of educational establishments. No further information is available at this time."

articles.title: ‘No early warning’: Zelenskyy says allies failed to alert Kyiv before Russian strikes; Rubio says US intel sharing never paused
articles.summary: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that Kyiv received no early warning from its international partners ahead of Russia’s latest ballistic
articles.body: Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed that Kyiv received no early warning from its international partners ahead of Russia’s latest ballistic missile attack on Monday. The overnight strikes across 11 Ukrainian regions damaged more than 10 energy facilities and left at least 5,50,000 households without electricity.The comments come as US secretary of State Marco Rubio denied that the US had paused some intelligence sharing with Ukraine.The attack, which involved ballistic missiles and drones, also killed one person and injured eight others in Kyiv, according to local authorities. The strikes damaged residential buildings, a medical facility, a school and a metro station, highlighting the continued threat to civilian infrastructure as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine’s energy network.In a post on X, Zelenskyy said Russia had launched 16 ballistic missiles in what he described as a deliberate attack on Kyiv and the surrounding region, alongside more than 200 drones, including jet-powered Shahed drones.“Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners,” he said.He added that the attacks extended beyond the capital, with strikes reported across regions ranging from Kharkiv and Dnipro to Volyn, Rivne and Odesa.“Overnight and this morning, Russia attacked energy facilities in the Vinnytsia, Volyn, Kirovohrad, Kyiv, Mykolaiv, Zhytomyr, Khmelnytskyi, Kharkiv, Ternopil, Odesa, and Rivne regions,” Zelensky said.“In this one night alone, more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities were damaged, and the lights went out for at least 550,000 families. Repair crews are working at the sites,” he added.Rubio on Monday denied that intelligence-sharing with Ukraine had been interrupted. “There's been no pause,” Rubio told NBC in Uzbekistan, adding, "I don't know where he's getting these things or why he's saying these things to the press. You should go back and ask him. There's been no pause."Ukraine’s Air Force said Russian forces had launched a large-scale overnight assault involving ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and 269 drones. Ukrainian air defences destroyed or suppressed 243 drones and four missiles, while strikes were recorded at 25 locations and debris fell at eight others, the force said.According to the Kyiv City Military Administration, the attack damaged a private medical facility and a metro station in the Desnianskyi district. Educational institutions and a sports facility were damaged in the Dniprovskyi district, while a fire broke out at a medical facility inside a 25-storey residential building in Solomianskyi district. Emergency services extinguished the blaze.Russia’s defence ministry also said it had carried out a “massive strike” using “ground-based high-precision weapons and strike drones”. It claimed to have hit military-industrial facilities, cruise missile storage sites and data centres in Ukraine, including locations in and around Kyiv allegedly linked to drone production and logistics.Ukraine’s deputy energy minister Artem Nekrasov said Russian attacks had targeted energy facilities in 11 regions. Rolling blackouts and electricity restrictions for industry and businesses had been introduced, he said in a post on Telegram.Zelensky also criticised what he described as inadequate support from Ukraine’s partners, particularly over air defence supplies and sanctions on Moscow.“Ukraine never wanted this war, and we have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to bring this war to a dignified end,” he said, adding that Ukraine had responded positively to every ceasefire proposal.“Putin not only doesn't want to end this war – he doesn't even want to take any steps toward de-escalation. EVERY ONE of our partners has experienced this firsthand when they heard Russia's refusals. And it is crucial to call things what they are. To call the aggressor an aggressor and help Ukraine defend lives. When deliveries of missiles for Ukraine's air defense are blocked while Russia is granted relief or delays in sanctions, this is, unfortunately, a denial of reality on the part of our partners", he said.You use AI every day. articles.title: Selena Gomez says vaping has affected her voice
articles.summary: The 34-year-old says vaping nicotine "a lot" permanently affected her singing and speaking voice.
articles.body:
Selena Gomez has said vaping nicotine has changed the way her voice sounds.

"I'm not gonna be able to change my voice," the singer, 34, said in a candid Instagram post on Sunday. "I vaped nicotine a lot."

"Nicotine is so hard to quit and I just wanted to say, if you're going through it, or if you're even trying to vape, it's just not worth it," she continued.

"It's so stupid and it changed my voice," she reiterated, then laughed: "So if you guys don't like listening to my voice, that's totally understandable. I don't mind. Just don't listen to it."

The singer and actress, who has the chronic autoimmune disease lupus, has previously suggested that the condition was affecting her vocal cords.

Asked about her voice in an Instagram Q&A last December, she said: "Sometimes things happen. I get weird. My throat kind of swells inside sometimes. That's all."⁠

Lupus flare-ups can cause inflammation around the larynx (voice box), which can cause your voice to become raspy and strained - similar to the symptoms of a cold.

Gomez's voice has also deepened with age, which is not uncommon. However, some fans have fixated on the change, posting compilation videos showing the evolution of her speaking style on YouTube.

In her Instagram video, the Only Murders In The Building star noted she had recently weaned herself off nicotine.

"I am really excited because I stopped and I just hope I can keep it up," she said.

"It's really hard, but I know if you are going through something you can get through it too. It sucks."

Evidence on some of the side effects of vaping are becoming a little clearer, although the long-term effects are still not known.

A recent report from doctors said vaping was linked to breathing problems, wheezing and coughing, dental issues, poor sleep, mental health problems and even eye symptoms.

Vaping isn't harmless - the nicotine in vapes is very addictive - which is why the NHS says children and non-smokers shouldn't take it up. But it has been shown to be an effective way to stop smoking.

Last month, the pop singer Lola Young said her " breathing feels like a chore " due to the effects of vaping.

Gomez first revealed her lupus diagnosis in a 2015 interview with Billboard.

The announcement came after she abruptly ended her 2013 tour to check herself into a rehab facility for treatment.

"I was diagnosed with lupus, and I've been through chemotherapy," she told the publication. "I locked myself away until I was confident and comfortable again.

"That's what my break was really about. I could've had a stroke."

Symptoms of lupus include muscle and joint pain, fever, rashes, chest pain, hair loss, kidney problems, fatigue and more.

In 2017, Gomez received a kidney transplant from her friend Francia Raisa, which helped move her lupus into remission for a period of time - although in her 2022 documentary Selena Gomez: My Mind And Me, the singer said she had had a flare-up in 2020.

However, after revealing her vaping habit, some people questioned her nicotine use, given the potential negative effect on her kidneys.

"Francia really gave this girl her kidney and she continued to smoke... oh wow," wrote one user on social media.

"To have someone generous enough to donate their kidney but still vape yourself into a nicotine addiction is absolutely wild," added another .

But most fans supported the star for being open about addiction.

"Selena Gomez being honest about nicotine addiction is a reminder that some habits are harder to quit than people realise," wrote MaxB on X .

"Proud of her for owning up to it and for wanting to do better," agreed Em.

articles.title: Possible wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane likely to be trees, say researchers
articles.summary: Researchers travelled to a remote Pacific Island to confirm whether an object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the mystery of the pilot's disappearance.
articles.body:
Researchers inspecting an object that some thought could have been the wreckage of Amelia Earhart's plane on a remote Pacific island say it is likely to be washed up trees.

The team travelled to a lagoon in the Taraia Peninsula on Nikumaroro, Kiribati, to confirm whether a shiny object first spotted on satellite imagery in 2020 solved the decades-long mystery of the pioneering pilot's disappearance.

But Purdue University, which has a leading role in the study, said the so-called Taraia Object "was likely a collection of large trees deposited along the peninsula's sandspit".

By the time the team arrived at the site a good portion of the debris had fragmented and washed away, leaving only a single Y-shaped segment, the university said.

Images of the Taraia Object - which Purdue University said was visible in photography dating back to 1938 - led researchers to wonder if it was the remnants of a small aircraft sitting in shallow waters.

"This mystery has been ongoing for 90 years and the mystery continues," said project director Rick Pettigrew, speaking from near the site of the object.

"The island has been holding on to its secrets and it continues to do so. I think eventually someone will find conclusive evidence here," he added.

Earhart's plane vanished without a trace in 1937 on the third-to-last leg of her attempt to fly around the world.

She had already successfully flown from California across South America, Africa and Asia in her twin-engine Lockheed Electra when she arrived in Lae, Papua New Guinea.

Earhart and her navigator Fred Noonan had planned to then travel towards Hawaii before returning to California.

But their plane vanished while trying to reach Howland Island, a remote uninhabited coral island about 400 miles (644km) from Nikumaroro, to refuel.

One theory is Earhart unintentionally navigated to Nikumaroro, where she ditched her plane and died a castaway.

The research team had travelled for five days by sea to reach Nikumaroro and was forced to spend several days on their ship following rough seas and strong winds, delaying their search on the island.

They spent four days onshore investigating the site.

articles.title: Around 1990, Zwolle clothing-rental owner Gregorius Halman pitched a castle; two years later, he won permission, then built four stories alone with recycled bricks.
articles.summary: Discover the incredible story of Gregorius Halman, who transformed his clothing-rental business into a 25-year architectural journey, building Olt Stoutenburght with reclaimed materials and Roman design inspiration in Friesland.
articles.body: Gregorius Halman ran a clothing-rental business in Zwolle, the Netherlands, and had no formal training in architecture or construction. He planned for a Roman-inspired structure with rounded walls, towers and curved architectural details, with local authorities taking about two years to approve the proposal, and construction beginning in 1992 in Blesdijke, a village in the Dutch province of Friesland. Halman used reclaimed bricks from demolished houses and roads, and the resulting structure, called Olt Stoutenburght, has a basement, four above-ground floors and a glass dome, according to the SPACES Archives.He studied Roman architecture during lunch breaksHalman's original idea was to build a castle as an extension of his house, and during lunch breaks from his clothing-rental business, he visited the public library in Zwolle to read books about Roman architecture to understand more about it. He wanted a design with flowing lines and rounded forms rather than the straight edges that were associated with much contemporary architecture, and developed the layout through his own ideas as construction progressed.Halman presented his proposal to local authorities around 1990 and received permission approximately two years later, with one condition restricting the towers to a maximum height of 27 metres, or about 89 feet. The castle's recorded construction date is 1992, and Halman was in his mid-40s when he began the project, according to the SPACES Archives, which documents independently built artistic environments around the world.The building stands at 84 Markeweg in Blesdijke, and its name, Olt Stoutenburght, is associated with Toutenburght, which is a former fortification in the surrounding region, while the Dutch word burght refers to a citadel. The name also incorporates stout, which historically could mean brave, although the word has a different meaning in modern Dutch.Reclaimed bricks and materials from old buildingsHow did Halman pull this off? He used old bricks that were recovered from demolished houses and roads as his main construction material, and also incorporated salvaged objects from other buildings into the castle's interior. The entrance doors came from an old Dutch prison, and a large conference table that had previously stood in a nearby town hall was added, while the fireplace in the central room came from an English country house. These pieces were incorporated into the structure instead of being discarded.The mixture of materials and shapes is a reflection of Halman's preference for design over strict historical accuracy. The official Olt Stoutenburght website describes the project as Halman's lifelong undertaking and says that he has worked with more than 250,000 bricks, and also records his practice of shaping and laying the bricks by hand. Friesland's official tourism website reported that the project was still ongoing in 2021, more than 25 years after construction began, and its listing describes the castle as a building made from reclaimed historical materials and inspired by Romanesque architecture.A construction project spanning decadesHalman developed the structure as he worked, and adjusted its details to match his ideas. The SPACES Archives records four floors above ground, with cellars that extend about two metres below the surrounding surface, while the roof features a glass dome, and the building includes spaces that were furnished with reclaimed objects. Halman viewed the building process itself as an important part of the undertaking, which made it different from a typical residential construction job. In interviews documented by SPACES, he described the pleasure he found in working with materials and developing the structure.The castle is now an established destination in Friesland, and visitors can arrange guided tours through its official website, which also advertises the property for photography, filming, weddings and meetings. Olt Stoutenburght remains associated with the same person who conceived it, more than three decades after construction began. Halman started with an idea for a castle beside his home, and then spent years assembling its walls, rooms and architectural details by hand.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: In 1994, a Mississippi woman bought a 432-acre farm later valued at $1.2 million; after marrying in 2004 and using the land to help finance their home, a divorce court ruled her husband had no ownership claim to it
articles.summary: A Mississippi woman has retained sole ownership of a 432-acre farm valued at approximately $1.2 million after her former husband challenged its status
articles.body: A Mississippi woman has retained sole ownership of a 432-acre farm valued at approximately $1.2 million after her former husband challenged its status during their divorce. In its October 13, 2026, decision, the Mississippi Court of Appeals upheld the lower court's ruling that the property remained hers because the evidence did not establish that it had been converted into a marital asset. According to the court's opinion published by Justia, the farm's use as security for a loan that helped finance their marital home did not automatically give her husband an ownership interest. The appeals court also upheld the allocation of additional land needed for the home's septic system.A farm purchased before marriageThe case, Wiley Bryant Harrison v. Ellen Trainor Harrison, arose from the couple's divorce and their disagreement over property division. Ellen Harrison purchased Butler Road Farm in 1994, a decade before marrying Wiley Harrison in 2004. The property covered approximately 432 acres and was valued at around $1.2 million. During the marriage, the farm was rented to a third party rather than used as the couple's residence. Following their separation, Ellen sought a divorce, citing habitual cruel and inhuman treatment. The Lee County Chancery Court granted the divorce and classified Butler Road Farm as her non-marital property.Wiley challenged the classification, arguing that the property's connection to their shared finances and his alleged work on the land entitled him to an interest in it. The dispute required the courts to determine whether the farm's status had changed during the marriage.Why the refinancing loan did not establish ownershipA central issue was a refinancing loan secured against Butler Road Farm. Both spouses signed the loan documents, and some of the funds were used to finance construction of their marital home in Saltillo, Mississippi. Wiley argued that using the farm to support the couple's household finances made it a marital asset. He also claimed to have performed work on the property, including removing bridges, which he suggested contributed to its maintenance and value.Ellen maintained that she managed the farm as a rental property and paid the mortgage instalments and property taxes. She testified that the refinancing loan was repaid using rental income, although the parties disputed whether Wiley contributed financially. The chancery court found insufficient evidence to establish that the farm had become marital property. The Court of Appeals agreed, concluding that signing a loan secured by the property did not, by itself, transfer ownership to Wiley.How Mississippi law treats separate propertyUnder Mississippi law, property acquired before marriage is generally considered non-marital. However, separate property can become marital under certain circumstances, including commingling with marital assets or being converted through the spouses' conduct and contributions. The court considered whether the refinancing arrangement and Wiley's alleged work justified changing the farm's classification. It concluded that the evidence did not demonstrate the necessary transformation.The judges also considered whether Wiley's efforts had contributed sufficiently to the property's value. The trial court had evaluated the conflicting testimony and found his claimed contributions inadequate to establish an ownership interest. The appeals court declined to disturb those findings. Its decision did not establish that premarital property can never become marital property. Rather, it confirmed that the evidence in this particular dispute did not justify treating the farm as jointly owned.Dispute over additional land near the homeThe husband also challenged the allocation of 2.19 additional acres from an adjoining 62-acre parcel. The chancery court awarded Ellen the marital home and the extra land because the home's septic system extended beyond the four-acre parcel on which the house stood. Ellen testified that the additional acreage was necessary to accommodate the system. Wiley did not contradict her testimony about its location or the need for the land.He argued that the court lacked sufficient evidence to justify the allocation and had not properly established the land's value. However, he did not provide a certified survey, appraisal or other evidence demonstrating that the valuation or allocation was incorrect. The Court of Appeals found that the evidence supported the lower court's decision. It upheld the additional acreage award as part of the overall division of property between the former spouses.Appeals court upholds the rulingOn October 13, 2026, the Mississippi Court of Appeals affirmed the chancery court's judgment, leaving Ellen with sole ownership of Butler Road Farm and upholding the distribution of the marital home and additional land. The ruling highlights the distinction between using property to support a marriage and establishing legal ownership of it. Although the farm helped secure financing for the couple's home, the court found that this arrangement alone did not make it a shared asset.The case demonstrates why courts examine when property was acquired, how it was managed and whether a spouse's contributions changed its legal status. In this instance, the refinancing loan and the husband's claimed work were insufficient to override the farm's classification as the wife's premarital property.You use AI every day. articles.title: A tiny green pottery shard links Great Zimbabwe to China; glass beads reveal the medieval African city's far-reaching trade networks
articles.summary: A small shard of jade-green pottery found at Great Zimbabwe has opened a window onto a journey that crossed continents and the Indian Ocean centuries ago.
articles.body: A small shard of jade-green pottery found at Great Zimbabwe has opened a window onto a journey that crossed continents and the Indian Ocean centuries ago. The fragment looks unlike the earth-brown pieces recovered from the same archaeological trench.Its smooth glaze led archaeologists to identify it as Longquan celadon, a prized type of Chinese pottery made in Longquan kilns in southeast China. According to the Secrets of the Dead PBS YouTube video, the discovery suggests goods reached the southern African city from a distant part of the world. The fragment is more than an unusual object. It offers a physical clue to the long-distance routes that connected Great Zimbabwe with traders and communities far beyond Africa.A Chinese pottery shard found at Great Zimbabwe reveals its distant originsThe fragment caught archaeologists’ attention because its colour and finish differed from the Earth-Brown pottery found elsewhere in the trench. Shadreck Chirikure is an archaeologist and the Edward Hall Professor of Archaeological Science at the University of Oxford. He points to the pale body beneath the glaze and describes the surface as ‘apple green’.The broken edge looks rough under magnification, while the intact glazed area appears smooth. Muchen Zhou is a DPhil student in Archaeology at the University of Oxford, examines the piece under an ultra-high-resolution microscope. The close view reveals how even the glaze is across the surface. The video explains that producing a glaze this smooth required firing at very high temperatures. The shard’s appearance offered the team a way to investigate where it was made and how far it travelled.Great Zimbabwe pottery fragment identified as Chinese Longquan celadonThe microscope examination helped the team identify the fragment as Longquan celadon, a Chinese pottery style recognised for its jade-green glaze. The video says this finish required firing at temperatures above 2,000°F.Muchen said, “Only China had the technology and then the engineering to fire at such a high temperature”. She identifies the piece as high-temperature pottery produced in southern China. The fragment is linked to the kilns of Longquan in southeast China. Its presence at Great Zimbabwe connects an object found in southern Africa to a pottery-making tradition.The discovery reveals the connections between Africa, Asia and the Middle EastThe pottery would have travelled a considerable distance before reaching Great Zimbabwe. The video describes how it could have passed through Southeast Asia and South Asia, then the Persian Gulf, before crossing the Indian Ocean.Longquan celadon was highly prized and traded in Europe and the Middle East, where it served as a sign of wealth and status. The shard offers a tangible reminder of the movement of goods between distant regions, linking a pottery-making centre in China with a settlement in southern Africa.Glass beads and imported goods show how trade shaped Great ZimbabweThe green pottery is not the only evidence of long-distance exchange emerging from the trench. As excavations continue, the team also finds large numbers of glass beads that were not made in southern Africa. The video describes glass items linked to Southeast Asia, India, the Middle East, and regions around Iran.Together, these objects suggest that Great Zimbabwe had contact with people and goods moving across continents and oceans. The video explains that trade brought wealth, attracted more people, and helped drive its expansion and population boom. The pottery fragment is part of a wider archaeological picture in which Great Zimbabwe was not an isolated settlement, but a place shaped by exchange with distant regions.You use AI every day. articles.title: Bereaved families could face 'unjust' tax bill after civil service pension delays
articles.summary: The chairman of Parliament's Public Accounts Committee says families should not be taxed through no fault of their own.
articles.body:
Bereaved families affected by severe delays paying out civil service pensions could face an "unjust" tax bill, the government has been warned.

Under HMRC rules, certain lump sum pension payments must be paid within two years of the pension scheme being notified of a death to remain tax-free.

Conservative MP Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, who chairs Parliament's Public Accounts Committee, said it was "unconscionable" some families could face a "death tax" through no fault of their own.

The Cabinet Office said that if delays caused a tax charge there were existing avenues to claim compensation, such as the Pensions Ombudsman.

However, the ombudsman is currently advising that standard complaints are only likely to be resolved within 18 months, with more complex cases facing a longer wait.

The Civil Service Pension scheme manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK.

Outsourcing firm Capita took over the administration of the scheme from a company called MyCSP in December 2025, saying it inherited a backlog of more than 86,000 cases.

Despite a two-year transition period to prepare for the takeover, problems have persisted and by February the backlog had grown to 120,000 cases.

Retired civil servants and bereaved families have been left waiting months for pension payments, with some struggling to pay bills.

Civil service pension backlog 'overwhelmed' Capita, boss says

Emergency loans offered to civil servants waiting on pensions

Retired civil servants left in pension limbo

According to the latest figures up to 30 September , 1,643 outstanding cases of bereavement or death in service are more than 100 days old.

Of these, only 301 are in scope to be paid within 15 days.

The PCS union, which represents civil servants, said that while not all these cases would ultimately be affected by the two-year tax rule, there were "serious questions" over how long they would remain unresolved.

If someone dies before the age of 75, a pension lump sum death benefit is only tax-free if it is paid within two years of the pension scheme first becoming aware of the death, and if the value is below the deceased's Lump Sum and Death Benefit Allowance.

The payment would be taxed at the same rate as the beneficiary's income tax rate.

Sir Geoffrey has written to Cabinet Office Minister Louise Haigh to urge the government to confirm the bereaved families affected will not face this "unjust financial penalty".

His letter came after BBC Radio 4's Money Box Live highlighted the potential tax liability.

Sir Geoffrey said "the chaos currently engulfing the Civil Service Pension Scheme means that the likelihood of death benefit payments being made within two years is slim".

He warned "a significant number" of family members "will be watching the clock quickly tick down to a year, as the maladministration of the scheme enters its tenth month".

He added: "This is an additional stress they should not have to bear."

Rob Wassell, 58, has been waiting almost two years for the lump sum from his brother's civil service pension, following his death.

On 22 October it will be two years since the pension scheme was notified of his death so if he does not receive the payment in just a few days times, it could face being taxed.

Rob, who contacted the BBC's Money Box programme about his case, said he had been phoning Capita with increasing "desperation" as his situation dragged on.

"It's a bitter pill to swallow to have to pay tax for something which was not my fault," he said.

"It creates unnecessary worry and anguish through the process, which is already in itself difficult."

Rob said he needed the money to cover the estate costs he had to pay for his brother and fill a £20,000 hole in his savings.

However, he said it was "heartbreaking" to hear of other cases where people needed the money just to survive.

Rob added that the idea that he might face "another battle" to recoup the tax through compensation made it feel like "you just want to give up".

Fran Heathcote, head of the PCS union, said it would be "a profound injustice" if families faced a further financial penalty because of Capita's failures.

"If that does happen, the government should be ashamed that families are being made to pay the price for failures that are entirely outside their control," she said.

A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office, which has overall responsibility for the Civil Service Pension Scheme, said: "The service levels following the move to Capita have been completely unacceptable and we are committed to ensuring no member is left financially worse off.

"We are continuing to hold Capita to account, including holding back nearly £10m in payments, and are doing everything in our power to ensure that individuals do not experience delays.

"If delays cause a tax charge, existing avenues for complaints can provide financial redress or compensation to cover losses."

A Capita spokesperson said: "We are deeply sorry for the frustration that the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme has caused members and their families.

"Our teams are working tirelessly to resolve outstanding cases as quickly as possible, with particular focus on people who have been waiting the longest and those facing financial hardship or challenging personal circumstances."

articles.title: In 2009–12, South Carolina turned 285 abandoned crab traps into oyster-reef bases; oysters grew within 7 months on experimental reefs
articles.summary: Discover how South Carolina is repurposing abandoned crab traps into effective oyster-reef bases, enhancing coastal ecosystems and preventing habitat loss in just months.
articles.body: If you walk along the beach of a South Carolina creek during low tide, you might notice the debris the water leaves behind. Tattered rope, broken dock planks, plastic bottles, and even a cube of rusty wire that was formerly used as blue crab bait. Crabbers often lose their traps. Storms push the wires out of place, boat propellers shatter them, and some are just left to sink. The problem is that, long after crabbers stop tracking it, a neglected trap still catches crabs, turtles and other animals that cannot escape.Between 2009 and 2012, government experts tested a few hundred of them. The Department of Natural Resources in South Carolina did not dump the retrieved traps. Instead, they sealed the vents, covered the wire with concrete and repurposed the traps as the basis for oyster reefs. Supported by a plan sponsored by NOAA and the Southeast Aquatic Resources Partnership, or SARP, the initiative had deployed 285 modified traps in coastal waters by December 2012. It is a technique that can work on soft, muddy ground where typical reef development is difficult. The study is forthright about its tradeoffs.A problem that keeps fishingBlue crab fishing is a big business for the state, with landings valued at over $6 million a year, according to S.C. Sea Grant. Storms, heavy tides, boat propellers and ordinary wear can tear the lines, and traps shift or vanish. They keep catching creatures, a behaviour called ghost fishing, even after settling into a marsh or channel. According to the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources’ terrapin studies page, more than a third of the hundreds of abandoned traps removed each year contain trapped animals.The oyster side of this narrative begins with a materials concern. Crushed oyster shell is the typical building block used in reef repair work, however it can be costly to purchase and inefficient in swampy areas. There’s a lot of soft mud in the state’s tidal creeks and not the hard surfaces young oysters need to settle on, SARP adds. A solid hand-wire basket offers the larvae something to grab onto.NOAA says the project aims to keep reefs healthy and reduce coastline erosion and habitat loss.The results of the testsA 2014 thesis by A. D. Kreutzer, cited in a 2019 PeerJ study, found that concrete-dipped crab traps drew more oysters than untreated ones, likely because the concrete adds a rough surface and may mimic the chemical cues oysters give off. So traps are not always an alternative to shell. They are a fallback where shell falls short.Mud was the more beneficial discovery. In a separate investigation, traps with recycled oyster shell previously seeded with live spat were deployed on firm and soft sand for nine months. They never became clogged, even in soft dirt. In the traps, juvenile oysters averaged about 26 mm on hard ground and 31 mm on mud, with survival rates of 38.5% and 34.6%. The author discovered that repurposed traps, particularly cement-coated ones, could facilitate oyster restoration in many locations where existing shell methods aren’t feasible.The field images provide a similar story. SARP’s project page shows an experimental reef at Dawho Cut where traps were set on 5 April 2011 and photographed on 10 November that year, around seven months later. The second demonstration reef identified as having high oyster recruitment and growth on the coated traps is Bears Bluff on Wadmalaw Island.Where it is todayShellfish biologists with the department stated they have been recycling obsolete and donated crab traps as reef material since 2011. More recently, a NOAA-funded effort has aimed to find and remove abandoned traps and recycle the recovered wire into new oyster habitat. Other coasts have had their own studies. A 22-month field experiment published in PeerJ compared concrete structures with crab traps on degraded oyster bars in northwestern Florida.Oysters settled faster on the concrete in the first year, but both proved viable. Both did best at lower intertidal elevations. That is also why placement matters. Most of the South Carolina results come from monitoring periods of nine months or less, so it remains to be seen how these reefs will fare across several seasons. In practice, for now, it is simple. Wire that once sat in the water killing wildlife is hauled out and put to work, giving oysters a place to begin.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Headline: In 2018, Iowa researchers made concrete conduct electricity; 10 heated slabs remained free of snow and ice during several winter seasons
articles.summary: Discover how Iowa researchers developed electrically conductive concrete that effectively prevents snow and ice accumulation during harsh winter conditions, promising efficient winter maintenance solutions.
articles.body: Researchers installed 10 electrically conductive concrete slabs in the south parking lot at Iowa Department of Transportation headquarters in Ames, Iowa. The experiment tested whether electrically powered pavement could stay warm enough to limit snow and ice accumulation. The InTrans project record says the slabs showed promising results during the 2018-2021 winter seasons. Heating performance was assessed through sensors during snow and ice events, while a programmable logic controller allowed the system to be operated and monitored remotely. The project was sponsored by the Iowa Department of Transportation and the Iowa Highway Research Board. The findings demonstrate how pavement materials and electrical systems could work together, but do not establish that the method can replace conventional treatment across an entire road network.How conductive concrete produces heat Ordinary Portland cement concrete is blended with conductive material, such as carbon fibre or steel shavings, which makes the pavement act as a resistive heating element. When electricity passes between electrodes embedded in the conductive layer, the material’s electrical resistance generates heat. The surface can then be warmed above freezing, which prevents the accumulation of snow and ice by melting them.As laid out in the Self-Heating Electrically Conductive Concrete Demonstration Project, the system is built around conductive concrete and embedded electrodes. The other components include wiring, conduits, and a power supply. The researchers tested different electrode configurations, and the standard concrete slabs served as control sections for comparison. Across the 10 slabs, measured power density ranged from 10.2 to 45.6 watts per square foot, averaging 24.6 watts per square foot. It would be remiss not to mention that these figures represent the power delivered per unit of surface and not the total electricity consumption, nor its operating cost or savings.The final report recommended further investigation before broad deployment because design requirements vary by application. For instance, a system intended for a bridge deck may need different considerations from one installed in a parking area or road.From a demonstration to wider infrastructure use The potential of the 10 electrically conductive concrete heated pavement system (ECON HPS) slabs extends beyond a parking lot because maintenance during winter can require ploughing and de-icing chemicals, consuming labour and equipment while creating corrosive and environmental effects. The AASHTO Innovation Initiative brief presents electrically conductive concrete heated pavement as a viable option for locations where operational problems can be created by snow and ice. The areas identified for applications include airports and high-foot-traffic areas managed by businesses or municipalities, along with road infrastructure such as bridges, ramps, tunnels, and rest areas.The system can be installed as an overlay on existing pavement or incorporated as the upper layer in a two-lift pavement design for new construction. That flexibility could let agencies consider the technology during rehabilitation or new projects. However, these are potential uses, not places where the Iowa demonstration tested the system, and the project provides evidence from one full-scale installation. AASHTO’s background material cites estimated US airline revenue losses associated with flight delays in 2019 and the quantity of de-icing chemicals used on roads in 2020. Those figures explain the scale of the problem; they are not measured savings from the conductive concrete installation. The brief also describes development work beyond the Iowa trial, which included two draft technical specifications and two patent applications. For transportation agencies, the next step is to determine where the system’s electrical requirements, construction design, and winter performance justify its use.You use AI every day. articles.title: Uber wins bid to throw out £340m lawsuits from black cab drivers
articles.summary: Claims that Uber misled TfL over its licence were thrown out because they were brought too late.
articles.body:
Uber has won its bid to throw out claims worth about £340m brought by thousands of London black cab drivers and two former private hire firms.

The claimants alleged the ride-hailing company gave Transport for London (TfL) misleading information when it first got a licence to operate in the capital in 2012.

But a High Court judge ruled the cases had been brought too late and dismissed them without considering whether the allegations were true.

Uber, which denied the claims, said it was pleased the court had thrown them out at the earliest opportunity.

About 13,000 drivers were seeking nearly £200m in damages, Reuters reported, while a claim on behalf of Kabbie and Iride, two private hire firms that have since closed, sought about £140m.

The lawsuits were filed in 2024, and Uber argued they fell outside the six-year limit for bringing such claims.

In a written ruling, Mr Justice Birt said the claimants could have discovered the alleged deception before 2018.

RGL Management, which ran the cases for the claimants, said it was very disappointed and was considering its options with the legal team.

Since gaining its licence, Uber has taken much of the trade once dominated by black cabs.

The company faces a separate case next week, when it challenges HM Revenue and Customs in a tax dispute worth more than £1bn.

articles.title: Prime Minister Andy Burnham visits Aberfan ahead of 60th anniversary
articles.summary: A total of 116 children and 28 adults were killed on 21 October 1966 when a colliery spoil tip collapsed.
articles.body:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has met a survivor of the Aberfan disaster, as well as others with connections to the tragedy, days ahead of the 60th anniversary.

Burnham visited the Aberfan memorial garden on Monday morning alongside Jeff Edwards, one of the last children to be brought out alive from the wreckage, and Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock.

"It's been 60 years since one of the most horrifying tragedies this country has ever seen. All of those children lost," Burnham said.

On 21 October 1966, 116 children and 28 adults were killed when a colliery spoil tip collapsed, catastrophically engulfing a primary school and surrounding houses.

The prime minister said the tragedy was something his mum and dad told him about when he was growing up, adding that he was there to "recognise the community" and what they had been through.

"The strength of the community today is something to see and something to feel," he said.

"To say also to them, I don't think Aberfan was treated properly by the authorities and that also needs to be recognised.

"Because at a moment like this, I think all of those things need to be said and it's right that the prime minister is here to say that to them."

Pupils from Caegarw Primary School in nearby Mountain Ash, Rhondda Cynon Taf, were on a visit to the memorial garden, built on the site of the destroyed Pantglas School, on Monday morning, unaware that the prime minister would also be there.

Burnham spent about 15 minutes in the memorial garden, before speaking to people who had gathered outside. He also visited a community centre.

He said coal tip safety, particularly in former mining communities in south Wales, was of "critical importance".

"It's of critical importance that we make sure that all of the remaining tips around Wales are safe indeed across the country," he said, adding he represented a former mining community in Makerfield near Manchester.

He said his government was providing around £140m to the Welsh government, who were "adding some extra funding themselves".

"There's an organisation that is being set up to manage all of these ongoing risks," he said.

Among the pupils he met was Ellis, 10, whose granddad travelled across the valley to Aberfan to help with the rescue effort.

"It means a lot to me and he tells me stories," said Ellis, who described visiting the memorial garden as "emotional".

Holly, aged 10 from Caegarw, also told the prime minister she had a personal connection with the tragedy.

"I told him about my godmother's daughter being one of the children who passed away in the disaster," she said.

"He said 'wow'. It means a lot for us to be here."

Burnham stopped to chat with local residents after visiting the garden before heading to the nearby community centre.

King Charles III, Queen Camilla and Prince William will visit the town on Wednesday to mark the anniversary, following on from the late Queen Elizabeth who visited Aberfan eight times.

articles.body: NEW DELHI: A routine security check at Delhi’s Jama Masjid Metro station turned into a dramatic chase when a passenger, allegedly trying to evade security, suddenly darted through the metal detector frame and rushed towards the escalator.But an alert CISF jawan sensed something was amiss and sprang into action, chasing the man down the staircase before catching hold of him near the platform. articles.title: Falling crucifix kills Ecuador priest during livestreamed church service
articles.summary: Heavy crucifix suddenly detaches from wall behind altar and strikes priest
articles.body:
A Catholic priest in Ecuador has died after he was fatally crushed by a falling crucifix while live-streaming evening mass.

The shocking accident occurred on Saturday at the Nuestra Senora del Perpetuo Socorro Church in Guayaquil, Ecuador's largest city, some 265km southwest of the capital.

Patricio Alfredo Sánchez Molinari was broadcasting the event live from his social media accounts when the mounted cross on the wall behind him fell suddenly, around 30 minutes into the stream.

Graphic footage of the mass showed a heavy crucifix hanging behind the altar detaching and falling onto the back of the priest's head.

The priest was facing the congregation at the time and did not appear to see it fall. The video showed he did not stand up again after being struck.

The priest was knocked below the altar and out of view, but recorded horrified worshippers shouting out and rushing to his aid.

"Father, Father! Call an ambulance!" people could be heard shouting just before the broadcast cut out. Others could be seen rushing towards the altar to help the stricken cleric.

Emergency services were immediately called to the scene, but first responders were unable to revive the priest. The video of the livestream was later taken down from the priest's page, but circulated widely on social media, NBC News reported.

The archdiocese of Guayaquil confirmed his death on Sunday, writing that Sanchez "has left to the House of the Father to enjoy his presence and glory".

"Eternal rest grant unto him, O Lord, and let perpetual light shine upon him. May he rest in peace. Amen," they wrote in a statement in Latin published on social media.

The archdiocese did not say what had caused the crucifix to fall or whether there would be an investigation.

It was unclear whether he was killed instantly or died later from injuries.

Sánchez belonged to the Congregation of the Most Holy Redeemer, a Roman Catholic religious order founded in 1732 with a presence in 80 countries, according to the Associated Press.

A Eucharist in his memory was scheduled for Sunday evening, the archdiocese said.

Local authorities were yet to comment on the incident, and it was not clear what caused the crucifix to fall.

In 2014, a 21-year old man died and his friend was injured after they were crushed by a crucifix erected in honour of Pope John Paul II in northern Italy . The same year, a mother of two died in Chicago, US, after a stone gargoyle fell three stories from an old church, striking her as she was taking a walk with her fiancé.

articles.title: Trump, Putin, Xi could hold a meeting in China; discuss end to Ukraine conflict: Moscow
articles.summary: A trilateral meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping could be held next month to
articles.body: A trilateral meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping could be held next month to discuss an end to the Ukraine conflict, Moscow announced on Monday.Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the meeting was possible on the sidelines of next month’s APEC summit in China, although the idea was yet to be finalised."Given that all three heads of state may potentially take part in the summit in China, the subject of such a hypothetical meeting was indeed raised. It was raised, but no specific proposals or agreements were discussed or put forward by anyone, either regarding the meeting itself or the possible agenda and content of that meeting," said Peskov.However, Kyiv is critical of the idea, stating Ukraine’s absence in such a meet would deliver results opposite to peace-making efforts.Ukrainian foreign minister Andrii Sybiha alleged the meeting would only encourage Putin to continue the conflict."A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Ukraine, the US, and Russia could help end the war sooner. A trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China, and the US would do only the opposite: encourage Putin to continue this war," he said in a post on X.Moscow acknowledged that a final peace deal wasn’t possible without Ukraine’s involvement.When asked whether Putin believed he could achieve a deal without Ukraine's participation, Peskov said it was obvious that Ukraine would need to be involved in any final peace deal."Of course, a final settlement is impossible without the participation of someone in Kyiv who is prepared to take responsibility," he said, as cited by Reuters.The last US-mediated peace ⁠talks were in February before the US and ⁠Israel began their Iran offensive.According to AFP, Putin has repeatedly refused meeting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy without a final peace agreement. He has also questioned Zelensky’s authority to sign such an agreement, citing the expiry of his five-year presidential term and the continuation of martial law.Ukraine has strongly rejected this position, arguing that Putin’s refusal to meet Zelensky shows he is not interested in ending the war, a claim dismissed by Moscow.You use AI every day.
